complaint.title: CED & RELUFA vs. SG Sustainable Oils Cameroon
complaint.subtitle: Intimidation and bribing issues in Cameroon
complainants: Centre pour l'Environnement et le Développement
complaint.allegations:
SGSOC, an affiliate of New York-based agriculture company Herakles, expressed its intention in 2013 to develop a large oil palm plantation and refinery in South West Cameroon. According to the complainants, SGSOC may have violated the OECD Guidelines anti-bribery provisions by intimidating and bribing community leaders, government officials and local citizens to gain land for their operations. They also assert the company has not worked in good faith with local communities, nor consulted them in accordnance with international Free, Prior, and Informed Consent standards.
CED/RELUFA maintained that SGSOC should address the allegations raised in the complaint either by publicly denying them or by investigating them, and requested that SGSOC create policies and procedures to regularly consult with the community members and members of civil society.
complaint.outcome:
In response to the complaint the company denied the allegations and stated that it considers its conduct to be fully consistent with the international guidelines. After its initial assessment issued in October 2013, the NCP offered its mediation services to assist the parties in seeking a mutually agreeable resolution to the issues raised. A local mediator was hired to assist with mediation and participated in-person in Yaounde, under the coordination of the U.S. Federal Mediation Conciliation Service (FMCS). The Office of the U.S. NCP observed the mediation.
The mediation was successfully concluded with an agreement between the parties. SGSOC agreed to receive a written request from the NGOs regarding the investigation of any past cases of alleged corruption, to investigate credible cases and respond in writing within three months. The company will also act with the intention to showing their good faith in opposing and taking action against any acts of corruption.
The parties further agree to meet again after SGSOC sends its first report of investigation to the complainants. The US NCP requested the parties to submit a follow-up reports identifying the status of the agreement and any impacts one year from the publication of its final statement.

case.title: Herakles Farms (SGSOC) Palm Oil Project and the Arrest of Nasako Besingi
case.place: Mundemba and Nguti area, Ndian and Kupe-Manenguba divisions, South West Region, Cameroon
case.point: Mundemba, where SEFE activists were arrested (Wikipedia coordinates)

lenders.name: Herakles Farms (New York), foreign investor
lenders.role: Its subsidiary SG Sustainable Oils Cameroon signed a 99-year lease for 73,086 hectares in 2009 (Wikipedia). IPS reports the project was linked to the Blackstone Group.

case.conditions: No lender is documented. A US agribusiness company obtained a 99-year land lease from the government for an industrial palm oil plantation and refinery (IPS; Wikipedia).
case.community: SGSOC began bulldozing forest and the cocoa and vegetable farms that communities depended on to build nurseries, without the presidential decree Cameroonian law requires and despite two court injunctions (IPS, 2012). The Oakland Institute and Greenpeace said the project could affect up to 45,000 people (IPS). Villagers' assemblies rejected the company's claims of local consent (Cultural Survival).
case.suppression: On 29 August 2012 Nasako Besingi, director of the local NGO SEFE, was pulled off his motorcycle and beaten by men he identified as Herakles junior managers (FIDH). On 14 November 2012 more than 15 armed gendarmes raided SEFE's office in Mundemba, where about 50 residents had come for campaign T-shirts, and arrested Besingi and five colleagues without a warrant; some local women were forcibly undressed by the gendarmes (FIDH). After a complaint by Herakles Farms he was prosecuted for publishing false news over an email describing the attack; on 3 November 2015 he was sentenced to a fine of 1 million CFA francs or three years in prison (FIDH; Wikipedia). He and the five colleagues were also prosecuted for holding an undeclared public meeting (FIDH).
case.outcome: Herakles withdrew the project from certification by the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil in August 2012 (Cultural Survival; IPS).

complaint.title: Greenpeace vs. Herakles Capital
complaint.subtitle: Disclosure violations by Herakles operating in Cameroon
complaint.concluded: 19 May 2014, Related complaints, Greenpeace vs. Herakles Farms
complaint.allegations: In March 2014 the US NCP received a request for review from the NGO Greenpeace alleging that Herakles Farms and Herakles Capital (Herakles), the former of which is a New York-based entity, had breached the disclosure provisions of the Guidelines in Cameroon. Specifically it was alleged that Herakles neglected to provide public documentation of its financial and operating results, financial contributions to All for Africa, and major share ownership and voting rights.
complaint.outcome: The NCP conducted an initial assessment of the specific instance and determined that the issues raised did not merit further examination. The NCP based its decision on the fact that the public documentation that Herakles provides on its website in large measure duplicates the relevant information that shareholders would expect from the annual report of a multinational corporation. The NCP therfore declined to offer its good offices for mediation and issued a statement detailing its decision and concluding the specific instance.

complaint.title: Jubilee Australia et al. on behalf of affected Morobe Province communities vs. Newcrest Mining Ltd and Harmony Gold (Australia) Pty Ltd
complaint.subtitle: Newcrest Mining and Harmony Gold’s proposed dumping of toxic mining waste in PNG
complainants: Centre for Environmental Law and Community Rights
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Papua New Guinea
complaint.concluded: 29 August 2025, Related complaints, Jubilee Australia et al. on behalf of affected Morobe Province communities vs. Harmony Gold (Australia) Pty Ltd and Newcrest Mining Ltd
complaint.allegations:
On 9 November 2022, Jubilee Australia, the Centre for Environmental Law and Community Rights, and the Evangelical Lutheran Church of PNG filed a complaint against Newcrest Mining and Harmony Gold (Australia) – both Australian mining companies – in relation to their proposal to dump toxic mining waste into the Huon Gulf in PNG’s Morobe Province. The complaint was lodged on behalf of 2,596 community members in Morobe Province.
The companies are joint partners in the Wafi-Golpu Joint Venture in PNG, which is proposing to construct and operate an underground copper-gold mine and associated ore processing. The complainants are opposed to the companies’ plan for the dumping of toxic mining waste into the ocean of the Huon Gulf.
The complaint makes several allegations against the companies, including:
Failure to obtain community consent for the proposal
Failure to provide an adequate environmental assessment of the proposal
Failure to respect human rights
Lack of due process in relation to Free Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) from the impacted communities
The complainants seek several remedies, including for the companies to publicly commit to abandon their proposal and to develop a new tailings management plan.
complaint.outcome:
On 1 August 2023, the Australian NCP published its initial assessment, deciding that the complaint merited further consideration and would be appropriate for ‘good offices’ within the OECD Guidelines. The NCP will proceed to offer its good offices to both parties. The NCP noted the complainant’s interest in engaging with the respondent companies on discussions around their concerns regarding the disposal of mining waste into the ocean via the two sites as currently proposed by the companies.
On 29 August 2025, the Australian NCP published its final statement. As the parties were unable to come to an agreement on the issues raised, the NCP undertook its own examination. Its its statement, the NCP made 28 recommendations to the companies for consistency with the Guidelines, as well as determinations that their activities do not comply with the standards in the (2011 version of the) OECD Guidelines, namely:
Failure to disclose key information regarding foreseeable risks
Inadequate human rights due diligence
Failure to address environmental impacts over the full lifecycle
Regarding critically endangered species, failure to operate ‘within the framework of laws, regulations and administrative practices in the countries in which they operate, and in consideration of relevant international agreements, principles, objectives, and standards, take due account of the need to protect the environment’ to ‘assess, and address…the foreseeable environmental…impacts…with a view to avoiding or, when unavoidable, mitigating them’
Failure to establish an appropriate system of environmental management
Failure to adopt a precautionary approach related explicitly to the due diligence associated with critically endangered species, and appropriate baseline development commensurate with the level of risk
The NCP was unable to make determinations as to the companies respecting international human rights law, specifically the right to FPIC, and their protection of the environment for the entirety of  the project.
Given the large number of recommendations by the NCP, the NCP recommended for the companies to develop an open and transparent plan, including timeframes and responsibilities for implementation, for all of the recommended actions into a coherent framework. The NCP said: “Noting that most of these activities relate to FPIC and due diligence, it is envisaged that all activities would be undertaken before the project receives its final approvals, and formally commences its operations. The initial plan should be developed within three months of the final report being released and should be disclosed publicly. An update should be provided at six months and twelve months.” The NCP’s recommendations related to the companies strengthening their human rights and environmental due diligence and FPIC processes, ensuring all baseline data used by the companies use recent data and apply best practice standards, further development of internal (disclosure) policies, addressing technical and scientific contentions, and reviewing relevant project documentation.

case.title: Lihir Gold Mine
case.place: Lihir Island, New Ireland Province, Papua New Guinea
case.point: Lihir mine on Lihir Island (EJAtlas point)

lenders.name: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA)
lenders.role: In fiscal year 1996, issued $10 million in political risk cover to R.T.Z. Overseas Holdings for part of its equity, and $66.6 million to a lender syndicate led by Union Bank of Switzerland, which lent $300 million to Lihir Gold Limited. MIGA called it its first project in Papua New Guinea.

companies.name: Lihir Gold Limited
companies.role: Project company that built and ran the mine

companies.name: RTZ (Rio Tinto)
companies.role: Equity investor covered by MIGA (R.T.Z. Overseas Holdings)

case.community: The project included moving area residents to new homes (MIGA). Coastal villagers depend on the sea for food and income, and the long-term effects of seabed waste on them are unknown (McKinnon, 2002).
case.suppression: In June 2015, landowners shut the mine over a benefits package pending since 2012; the government sent a heavily armed police squad to reopen it (EJAtlas, citing ABC News). No injuries or arrests are reported.
case.ecosystem: Tailings are piped into the sea at 125 m depth, 1.5 km offshore, and spread across the seabed down to 1,600 m. Barges dump 1,400 to 4,600 tons of waste rock an hour about 1 km offshore. A 2015 study found far fewer seabed animals at 800 to 2,020 m depth near Lihir than at reference sites, and called the impacts of active tailings deposition severe.
case.outcome: Disputes with landowners have halted mining at times, including in 2012 (EJAtlas, citing the Financial Times). Waste disposal into the sea continues.

complaint.title: Friends of the Earth Japan and WALHI vs. Marubeni Corporation
complaint.subtitle: Impacts from the Cirebon coal power project in Indonesia
complaint.concluded: 13 February 2024, Related complaints, Friends of the Earth Japan and WALHI vs. JERA Co., Inc.
complaint.allegations:
On 23 May 2017, a complaint was filed to
the
Japan
ese NCP against Marubeni Corporation and JERA Co., Inc.  by
Friends
of
the
Earth
Japan
and Wahana Lingkungan Hidup Indonesia (WAHLI), representing local communities in Indonesia, for adverse impacts linked to
the
Cirebon coal-fired power project in West Java.
The
complainants allege that
the
companies, involved in a joint venture connected to the power project, are in breach
of
the
OECD Guidelines due to their failure to obey domestic laws and refrain from seeking or accepting exemptions not contemplated in
the
statutory or regulatory framework.
The
complaint states that since
the
construction
of
Unit 1
of
the
Cirebon coal-fired power project  in Indonesia, local communities have experienced significant damage to
the
ir livelihoods and incomes. Despite community protests and
the
impacts already suffered
the
re is work underway to begin building Unit 2
of
the
Cirebon coal-fired power plant.
The
project is expected to be operational in 2021 and to fur
the
r damage
the
livelihoods
of
the
fishermen in
the
area, who have yet to receive any livelihood restoration from Unit 1
of
the
project and have not been informed
of
any plans related to Unit 2.
The
complainants allege illegalities around
the
project’s environmental permit and
the
designated spatial plan.
The
complainants are asking
the following from the
Japan
ese NCP:
That
the
companies adhere to
the
OECD Guidelines.
That all project related activities for Unit 2 stop until a final court decision is made to ensure
the
project is compliant with laws and regulations.
That
the
company refrains from seeking or accepting exemptions.
That
the
company encourages West Java provincial government to withdraw its appeal to
the
high court or
the
Supreme Court, and make efforts to comply with
the
Indonesian laws and regulations.
complaint.outcome:
On 24 June 2017, the Japanese NCP officially accepted the complaint.
On 2 February 2018, the Japanese NCP accepted the complaint for further consideration. The NCP did not publish its initial assessment.
The long duration between the complaint being filed (May 2017), the NCP’s official acceptance of the complaint (June 2017), and the NCP’s initial assessment (February 2018) was a significant issue for the complainants. This complaint raised issues with the legality of the environmental permit for the project, but before the NCP published its initial assessment a new permit had been issued (in July 2017) and the project financiers had started their loan disbursement (in November 2017). Therefore many of the issues the complainants sought to address through their complaint (including that the project stop before the final court decision was made) had occurred before the assessment was even published.
The NCP offered its good offices to the parties. In December 2018, the companies replied to the NCP, stating that they were unable to answer the NCP’s offer of good offices due to ongoing Indonesian proceedings involving the complainants. In March 2019, the companies notified the NCP of the finalisation of proceedings in their favour; however, they continued to refuse to accept the NCP’s offer until the complainants confirmed that the proceedings had been terminated. In August 2019, the complainants informed the NCP that they had filed a request for a retrial of the Indonesian case. In December 2019, the Japanese NCP met separately with the parties about the issues in the NCP complaint and proceedings in Indonesia. Ultimately, the companies refused to engage in the NCP process unless and until the complainants terminated all legal proceedings in Indonesia against them.
In May 2021, the NCP asked the complainant whether a timeline should be set for the companies’ engagement in the NCP process. The complainants replied that they would withhold their position regarding acceptance or rejection of good offices until local investigations related to corruption at the power plant were completed. The NCP held another in-person meeting with the complainants in May 2023.
On 19 September 2023, the Japanese NCP notified all parties that it considered them unwilling to engage in the NCP process and if no progress was made in the following two months, the NCP would terminate the complaint process and issue its final statement. As no objection was received from any of the parties, the NCP published its final statement on 13 February 2024. The NCP recommended “that the Enterprises Involved continue to ensure the observance of the Guidelines, and to engage with the local community and residents, including the Complainants.”
The complainants note that the NCP’s role is more than just to offer its good offices (mediation) for dialogue. The NCP should also proactively review companies’ compliance with the OECD Guidelines and make clear recommendations on the implementation of the Guidelines by companies.

case.title: Jawa-1 gas power plant: fishers' catch and tenant farmers
case.place: Cilamaya, Muara and Blanakan villages, Karawang and Subang, West Java, Indonesia
case.point: Cilamaya, Karawang, site of the Jawa-1 power plant (OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Approved 29 August 2018 as a direct loan of up to US$250 million and a parallel loan of up to US$150 million from the Leading Asia's Private Infrastructure Fund that ADB manages; the final package was US$185 million from ordinary capital and US$120 million from that fund (CRP).

lenders.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation and NEXI-insured commercial banks
lenders.role: Other lenders to the project company (ADB Management, cited by CRP).

lenders.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC)
lenders.role: Loan agreement of 18 October 2018 with a maximum JBIC portion of about US$604 million, within co-financing of about US$1,312 million with Mizuho, MUFG and others, the banks' part covered by NEXI (JBIC).

companies.name: PT Pertamina
companies.role: Project sponsor, Indonesia's state oil and gas company

case.conditions: The loans financed a 1,760 MW gas-fired power plant with an undersea gas pipeline, seawater pipelines and a floating storage unit, under a 25-year power purchase agreement with the state utility PLN (CRP). ADB's Report and Recommendation of the President for the Jawa-1 project sets out obligations the borrower and sponsors took on. The borrower was to submit quarterly unaudited and annual audited financial statements together with environmental and social monitoring reports, and to report regularly to ADB on labour measures and periodically on gender measures. "The sponsors will recruit experienced safeguards staff to ensure effective implementation", and on noise the sponsor "has agreed to  …[truncated]
case.community: Complainants said at least 284 households depend on fishing and that 68 household heads interviewed had lost 40–80% of fishing income to restricted zones, turbid water and damaged gear. The CRP calculated that pre-project catches at one fish auction site (68,319 kg in 2015, 48,946 kg in 2016, 37,074 kg in 2017) averaged more than twice the 2021–2024 average, with 8,981 kg in 2021. Tenant farmers say they were each paid Rp150,000 in 2016 and asked to sign an agreement not to complain. Residents of Karanganyar live beside the plant without a buffer zone (CRP).
case.outcome: The CRP found preliminary evidence of non-compliance and of direct and material harm to fishers' catch, and the ADB Board authorized a compliance review on 27 January 2026 (CRP).

complaint.title: Employees of Kawaguchi Manufacturing vs. Kawaguchi Manufacturing, Sony and Panasonic
complaint.subtitle: Labour rights violations at supplier to Sony and Panasonic
complaint.allegations:
On 27 December 2024, 251 workers of Kawaguchi Manufacturing Sdn. Bhd. (“Kawaguchi Manufacturing”), represented by lawyers, filed a complaint against Kawaguchi Manufacturing, Sony Corporation (“Sony”) and Panasonic Corporation (“Panasonic”) at the Japanese NCP. The complaint concerns alleged labour rights violations at Kawaguchi Manufacturing in Malaysia and their links to Sony and Panasonic.
The complainants allege that workers at Kawaguchi Manufacturing have experienced violations indicative of forced labour, including non-payment of wages, confiscation of passports, intimation and charging of high recruitment fees, among other labour rights violations. They allege that Sony and Panasonic, who sourced from Kawaguchi Manufacturing, failed to adequately engage with the workers and provide for remediation. They allege that Sony and Panasonic discontinued their business with Kawaguchi Manufacturing instead, which drove Kawaguchi Manufacturing to cease operations.
The complainants are seeking repayment of unpaid wages and recruitment fees and compensation for mental damage.
complaint.outcome:
On 27 June 2025 and 17 July 2025, Sony and Panasonic respectively submitted statements to the Japanese NCP in mid-2025 explaining their due diligence policies and actions in relation to the issues raised in the complaint. Sony stated that its investigation, including a third-party audit, had confirmed violations of its Supply Chain Code of Conduct at Kawaguchi Manufacturing and that it had implemented remedial measures for the workers. Panasonic stated that it had concluded Kawaguchi Manufacturing’s treatment of the workers to be in breach of Panasonic’s human rights and labour policies and supply chain guidelines, and that it had exercised leverage to ensure remedy from Kawaguchi Manufacturing while independently reimbursing recruitment fees paid by workers.
On 17 July 2025 and 22 September 2025, the complainants informed the NCP that an agreement had been reached with Sony and Panasonic respectively and that they were withdrawing the complaints against both companies.
On 24 April 2026, the Japanese NCP issued its Final Statement detailing the above developments.

case.title: East Coast Rail Link: homes cleared and flooded at Gombak
case.place: Kampung Sungai Chinchin and Desa Mukmin, Gombak Utara, Selangor, Malaysia
case.point: Kampung Sungai Chinchin, Gombak, in the Selayang municipal area (OpenStreetMap via Nominatim); approximate for the case as a whole, which covers villages across Gombak Utara including Desa Mukmin and Kampung Sungai Salak

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Preferential buyer's credit to Malaysia Rail Link Sdn Bhd for Phase 1 of the East Coast Rail Link. AidData's records, read on 15 November 2026, say China Eximbank and Malaysia Rail Link signed a preferential buyer's credit worth RMB 61.88 billion (RM 39.1 billion) on or around 1 April 2017, and that the loan reportedly carried a 20-year maturity, a 7-year grace period and a fixed 3.25% interest ra …[truncated]

companies.name: China Communications Construction Co. (CCCC)
companies.role: Engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning contractor for the railway, working in Malaysia as China Communications Construction (ECRL) Sdn Bhd, which is one of three defendants in a 2026 High Court claim over damage to a house at Gombak (AidData; New Straits Times)

companies.name: Malaysia Rail Link Sdn Bhd (MRL)
companies.role: Borrower and owner of the railway; offered the ex-gratia money at Desa Mukmin with the state government, and agreed to cover rent for 21 households at Sungai Chinchin and repairs to homes and roads there (AidData; Sinar Harian; Selangor Journal)

case.conditions: The credit was to pay 85% of the cost of the 1 November 2016 commercial contract between Malaysia Rail Link and China Communications Construction Company, worth RMB 72.8 billion (RM 46 billion), so the money was spent with the lender's own state contractor. 60% was to be made available in renminbi and 40% in ringgit. The Government of Malaysia gave a sovereign guarantee. When Malaysia cancelled the project in August 2018, China Eximbank told the new government it could either renegotiate the contracts or pay termination costs of about RM 21.78 billion; the government renegotiated, and a supplemental agreement on 12 April 2019 cut the cost from RM 65.5 billion to RM 44 billion and set up a 50 …[truncated]
case.community: A census by Selangor's Department of the Director General of Lands and Mines on 21 November 2023 confirmed 135 structures in the railway's path at Desa Mukmin in Gombak, and that those 135 structures held 157 heads of household. The department and the Gombak District and Land Office issued an order to clear the site on Wednesday 13 December 2023, with a deadline of 15 January 2024. The payments offered to the owners and tenants told to vacate were RM 3,000 in moving costs, RM 1,500 a month in rent for 24 months and compensation for the structure, with a choice of 49 Rumah Selangorku units at Bandar Tasik Puteri priced at RM 79,000 or places in the state's SmartSewa rental programme at two sites, 40 units at Blok Temenggung and 240 at Sri Damai. Two residents said they accepted the order, one of them that the RM 3,000 eased the move (Sinar Harian). Residents said they were told in late November that they had 20 days to leave, and that the government planned to demolish their homes and about 100 others in the village; officers of the lands and mines department and a spokesperson for China Communications Construction (ECRL) declined to answer questions about the short notice, and the  …[truncated]
case.ecosystem: Residents at Kampung Sungai Salak said flash floods began after trees and the hillside behind the village were cleared for the works, and that floods now follow within an hour of rain (Malaysiakini). A private geologist engaged by one Gombak family in August 2024 reported high water saturation in the hillslope beside their house, and a later soil study commissioned by the family concluded the chance of the slope collapsing was very high (New Straits Times).
case.outcome: The Selangor government, with Malaysia Rail Link, handed the ex-gratia payments to the Desa Mukmin recipients at a ceremony at Dewan Beringin Sri Gombak on the Thursday after the clearance order of Wednesday 13 December 2023 (Sinar Harian, 14 December 2023; The Star, 18 December 2023). A retention pond was ordered for Sungai Chinchin in October 2024, and Malaysia Rail Link committed to suspending work there on Sundays and on days such as examination periods (Selangor Journal). A couple at Gombak filed a RM 1.33 million claim in the High Court on 24 April 2026 against China Communications Construction (ECRL) Sdn Bhd, Malaysia Rail Link and the Selayang Municipal Council, saying hillslope work since early 2024 made their house shake. They said a dilapidation survey was done only in February 2024 after repeated complaints, that the contractor and Malaysia Rail Link told them the environmental assessment and site investigation reports were in the public domain and they had to find them themselves, that the municipal council ordered a full study in early 2025 while Malaysia Rail Link said in March 2025 that the existing studies were enough, that a letter of demand in October 2025 was re …[truncated]

complaint.title: ACF et al.  vs ANZ Bank
complaint.subtitle: ANZ Bank’s facilitation of destructive forestry in PNG
complainants: Centre for Environmental Law and Community Rights
complaint.concluded: 13 October 2006, Related complaints, Green Party of New Zealand vs. ANZ Bank
complaint.allegations:
The complainants allege that ANZ Bank financially supports logging companies engaged in human rights abuses and environmental destruction in Papua New Guinea (PNG). Specifically, the complaints state that ANZ is “actively facilitating and supporting” the PNG operations of Malaysian logging giant Rimbunan Hijau (RH), a company whose operations involve “serious human rights abuses, environmentally devastating logging practices and repeated, serious illegal conduct” including:
By failing to take basic steps to ensure that its clients respect human rights, ANZ becomes closely associated with violations of those rights.
While ANZ has discussed community concerns with RH on these issues, this engagement has not demonstrated positive outcomes and is likely to be ineffective, as it does not occur within an articulated and binding framework of acceptable minimum environmental and human rights standards required as a condition for doing business with the bank.
ANZ has not adopted a system of environmental management appropriate to its business in that it has not adopted forestry and human rights policies that set acceptable minimum standards for client engagement, in contrast to a number of other multinational financial institutions.
Two OECD Guidelines complaints against ANZ have been filed: the first at the Australian NCP (ANCP) by ACF et al. and the second at the New Zealand NCP (NZ NCP) by the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand.
complaint.outcome:
After filing the first complaint in August 2006, ACF submitted supplementary evidence to the ANCP regarding the existence of an investment nexus between ANZ and RH in September 2006.
In October 2006, the ANCP rejected the complaint, claiming that ANZ’s loans and guarantees do not constitute an “investment nexus” between the bank and the logging company. The ANCP also claimed it was unable to ascertain whether ANZ’s degree of influence is sufficient to trigger the supply chain provision in the Guidelines.
ACF responded by stating its disappointment in the ANCP’s highly restrictive interpretation of the “investment nexus”. According to ACF, the Australian NCP excluded consideration of the complaint despite an undisputed debt financing link between ANZ Bank and the logging company. In addition, the rejection appears to be inconsistent with other complaints in which debt financing relationships have triggered the Guidelines’ complaint procedure.
The second complaint in New Zealand was rejected by the NZ NCP in February 2008. The NCP argued that, given the lack of a sufficient link between RH and ANZ’s New Zealand-based business and the previous examination of the issue by the Australian Government, further examination of the complaint was not warranted and would not contribute to the purposes and effectiveness of the Guidelines.

cmp_key: ncp:ACF et al.  vs ANZ Bank

case.title: Phnom Penh Sugar and the ANZ Loan
case.place: Thpong and Oral districts, Kampong Speu, Cambodia
case.point: Thpong district, site of the plantation and refinery

lenders.name: ANZ Royal Bank (Australia and New Zealand Banking Group)
lenders.role: Provided significant financing to Phnom Penh Sugar Company for its plantation and refinery, according to confidential assessment reports leaked in January 2014 (Inclusive Development International); the Australian NCP found ANZ could have known the risks from public information (OECD Watch).

companies.name: Phnom Penh Sugar Company
companies.role: Owner and operator of the plantation and refinery

case.conditions: ANZ lent to the sugar company while it was in conflict with more than 1,100 families in 21 villages (Inclusive Development International).
case.community: More than 1,500 families were forcibly displaced from their farms and more than 100 families from their homes; crops were destroyed and protected forest cleared (Inclusive Development International). The complaint was filed for 681 families and alleged military-backed land seizures, arrests and intimidation of villagers between 2010 and 2011, and child labour (OECD Watch).
case.suppression: Complainants alleged arbitrary arrests and intimidation of villagers (OECD Watch).
case.outcome: In June 2018 the Australian NCP found considerable shortcomings in ANZ's human rights policies and procedures but gave no guidance on redress. In February 2020, through the NCP, ANZ agreed to contribute the gross profit it earned from the loan; the money was distributed to 1,096 families, and in November 2021 ANZ launched a grievance mechanism (OECD Watch; Inclusive Development International).
case.killed_note: The complaint alleged dangerous working conditions that resulted in the death of several workers; no number is given, so none are counted.
